title: Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare
author: E. Nesbit
estimatedTime: About 3 hours; each story takes minutes
openingText: Hermia and Lysander were lovers; but Hermia’s father wished her to marry another man, named Demetrius.
about:
Edith Nesbit (1858–1924), the author of *The Railway Children*, retold twenty of Shakespeare’s plays as short prose stories. This volume opens with a preface and a brief life of Shakespeare. It then tells, in turn, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, The Tempest, As You Like It, The Winter’s Tale, King Lear, Twelfth Night, Much Ado About Nothing, Romeo and Juliet and twelve more, ending with All’s Well That Ends Well.

The stories keep the plots, the main characters and some of Shakespeare’s best-known lines, but they are told in plain narration, with the speeches often summarised. This is a retelling for young readers, not a substitute for the plays. It works as a first meeting with each play or a quick reminder of the plot.

whyItMatters.title: The plots in a few pages
whyItMatters.body: Each play is reduced to a few pages, so the shape of the story shows clearly. The retellings make it easy to see how often Shakespeare uses disguise, mistaken identity and a lost child found again. Reading several in a row shows his habits.

whyItMatters.title: A way into the plays
whyItMatters.body: Some of the lines people know from the plays appear here inside the story. A reader who has met Lear or Hamlet this way can approach the full play with the plot already in mind.

whyItMatters.title: What a retelling leaves out
whyItMatters.body: Nesbit shortens, tidies and sometimes softens. Comparing her version with the play shows what a prose retelling keeps and what it cannot carry, especially the poetry.

angleCards.title: Pick a play and compare
angleCards.text: Read Nesbit’s version of a play you know and note what she keeps, shortens or changes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare to see what a prose retelling keeps and loses from the plays.

angleCards.title: Collect the patterns
angleCards.text: Note recurring devices such as disguise, shipwreck, mistaken identity and forgiveness across the stories.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare to notice the plot patterns Shakespeare repeats.

angleCards.title: Meet the plays you don’t know
angleCards.text: Read the stories of the lesser-known plays, such as Pericles or Cymbeline, before looking at the plays themselves.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare to get to know the less familiar plays.

angleCards.title: Read the preface
angleCards.text: Read Nesbit’s preface and the life of Shakespeare and ask who her reader is meant to be.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare to understand who Nesbit was writing for and why.
